questions.stem:
Tessa owns a small clothes shop in a seaside town. She records the weekly sales figures, $£w$, and the average weekly temperature, $t°\mathrm{C}$, for 8 weeks during the summer.
The product moment correlation coefficient for these data is $-0.915$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Stating your hypotheses clearly and using a 5% level of significance, test whether or not the correlation between sales figures and average weekly temperature is negative.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: $\mathrm{H_0}: \rho=0$   $\mathrm{H_1}: \rho<0$
M1: for the critical value: sight of $\pm 0.6215$ or any cv such that $0.5<|cv|<0.75$
A1: must reject $\mathrm{H_0}$ on basis of comparing $-0.915$ with $-0.6215$ (if $-0.915<-0.6215$ is seen then A0 but may use $|r|$ o.e. which is fine) and mention "negative", "correlation/relationship" and at least "$w$" and "$t$"
Critical value: $-0.6215$ (Allow any cv in range $0.5<|cv|<0.75$)
$r<-0.6215$ so significant result and there is evidence of a negative correlation between $w$ and $t$ (3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Suggest a possible reason for this correlation.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) B1: for a suitable reason to explain negative correlation using the context given, e.g. "As temperature drops people are more likely to go shopping (than to the beach)"; e.g. "As temperature increases people will be outside rather than in shops". A mere description in context of negative correlation is B0
SO: e.g. "As temperature increases people don't want to go shopping/buy clothes" is B0; e.g. "Less clothes needed as temp increases" is B0
e.g. As temperature increases people spend more time on the beach and less time shopping (o.e.) (1)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Tessa suggests that a linear regression model could be used to model these data.
(c) State, giving a reason, whether or not the correlation coefficient is consistent with Tessa's suggestion.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) B1: for a suitable reason e.g. "strong"/"significant"/"near perfect" "correlation", $|r|$ close to 1 and saying it is consistent with the suggestion. Allow "yes" followed by the reason.
Since $r$ is close to $-1$, it is consistent with the suggestion (1)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) State, giving a reason, which variable would be the explanatory variable.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) B1: For identifying $t$ and giving a suitable reason. Need idea that "$w$ depends on $t$" or "$w$ responds to $t$" or "$t$ affects $w$" (o.e.). Allow $t$ (temperature) affects the other variable etc. Just saying "$t$ is the independent variable" or "$t$ explains change in $w$" is B0. N.B. Suggesting causation is B0 e.g. "$t$ causes $w$ to decrease"
$t$ will be the explanatory variable since sales are likely to depend on the temperature (1)

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Tessa calculated the linear regression equation as $w=10\,755-171t$
(e) Give an interpretation of the gradient of this regression equation.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) B1: for a description that conveys the idea of rate per degree Celsius. Must have 171, condone missing "£" sign.
Every degree rise in temperature leads to a drop in weekly earnings of £171 (1)

questions.stem:
In an experiment a group of children each repeatedly throw a dart at a target.
For each child, the random variable $H$ represents the number of times the dart hits the target in the first 10 throws.
Peta models $H$ as $\mathrm{B}(10,0.1)$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State two assumptions Peta needs to make to use her model.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: for stating that the probability (or possibility or chance) of a dart hitting the target is constant (or fixed or same) (from child to child and for each throw by each child) (o.e.)
B1: for stating that the throws of each of the darts are independent (o.e.) ["trials" are independent is B0] (2)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Using Peta's model, find $\mathrm{P}(H \geqslant 4)$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (b) B1: $[\mathrm{P}(H \geqslant 4)=1-\mathrm{P}(H \leqslant 3)=1-0.9872=0.012795\ldots=]$ awrt $0.0128$ (found on calculator) (1)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
For each child the random variable $F$ represents the number of the throw on which the dart first hits the target.
Using Peta's assumptions about this experiment,
(c) find $\mathrm{P}(F=5)$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for a probability expression of the form $(1-p)^4 \times p$ where $0<p<1$
A1: for awrt $0.0656$
$\mathrm{P}(F=5)=0.9^4 \times 0.1=0.06561=$ awrt $0.0656$
SC: Allow M1A0 for answer only of 0.066 (2)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Thomas assumes that in this experiment no child will need more than 10 throws for the dart to hit the target for the first time. He models $\mathrm{P}(F=n)$ as
$\mathrm{P}(F=n)=0.01+(n-1) \times \alpha$
where $\alpha$ is a constant.
(d) Find the value of $\alpha$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: for setting up the distribution of $F$ with at least 3 correct values of $n$ and $\mathrm{P}(F=n)$ in terms of $\alpha$. (Can be implied by 2nd M1 or 1st A1)
M1: for use of sum of probs $=1$ and clear summation or use of arithmetic series formula. (Can be implied by 1st A1) (allow 1 error or missing term)
A1: for a correct equation for $\alpha$
A1: for $\alpha=0.02$ (must be exact and come from correct working)
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline n & 1 & 2 & \ldots & 10\\ \hline \mathrm{P}(F=n) & 0.01 & 0.01+\alpha & \ldots & 0.01+9\alpha\\ \hline\end{array}$
Sum of probs $=1 \Rightarrow \frac{10}{2}[2\times 0.01+9\alpha]=1$
[i.e. $5(0.02+9\alpha)=1$ or $0.1+45\alpha=1$] so $\alpha=0.02$ (4)

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Using Thomas' model, find $\mathrm{P}(F=5)$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) B1ft: for value resulting from $0.01+4\times\text{"their } \alpha\text{"}$ (provided $\alpha$ and the answer are probs)
Beware: If their answer is the same as their (c) (or a rounded version of their (c)) score B0
$\mathrm{P}(F=5|\text{Thomas' model})=0.09$ (1)

parts.label: f
parts.text:
(f) Explain how Peta's and Thomas' models differ in describing the probability that a dart hits the target in this experiment.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(f) B1: for a suitable comment about the probability of hitting the target
ALT: Allow idea that Peta's model suggests the dart may never hit the target but Thomas' says that it will hit at least once (in the first 10 throws).
Peta's model assumes the probability of hitting target is constant (o.e.) and Thomas' model assumes this probability increases with each attempt (o.e.) (1)

Charlie is studying the time it takes members of his company to travel to the office.
He stands by the door to the office from 08 40 to 08 50 one morning and asks workers, as they arrive, how long their journey was.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State the sampling method Charlie used.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) B1: Convenience or opportunity [sampling] (1)

parts.label: b
parts.text:

(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) B1: Quota [sampling] ("Stratified" or "systematic" or "random" are B0B0)
B1: e.g. Take 4 people every 10 minutes. Requires suitable strata or categories e.g. time slots, departments, gender, age groups, distance travelled etc. Suggestion of randomness is B0 (2)

parts.label: c
parts.text:

(c) State the data selection process Taruni used.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (c) B1: Census (1)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Taruni's results are summarised by the box plot and summary statistics below.

$n=95 \quad \sum x=4133 \quad \sum x^2=202\,294$

(d) Write down the interquartile range for these data.
(1)

parts.label: e
parts.text:
(e) Calculate the mean and the standard deviation for these data.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) B1: for a correct mean (awrt 43.5)
M1: for a correct expression for the sd (including $\sqrt{\ }$) ft their mean
A1: for awrt 15.4 (Allow $s=15.4667\ldots$ awrt 15.5)

$\sigma_x=\sqrt{\frac{202\,294}{95}-\mu^2}=\sqrt{236.7026\ldots}=15.385\ldots$ awrt $15.4$ (min) (3)

parts.label: f
parts.text:
(f) State, giving a reason, whether you would recommend using the mean and standard deviation or the median and interquartile range to describe these data.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(f) B1: for acknowledging outliers or skewness are a problem for mean and sd ("extreme values"/"anomalies" OK). May be implied by saying median and IQR not affected by\ldots We need to see mention of "outliers", "skewness" and the problem so "data is skewed so use median and IQR" is B0 unless mention that they are not affected by extreme values or mean and standard deviation can be "inflated" by the positive skew etc

(3)

The lifetime, $L$ hours, of a battery has a normal distribution with mean 18 hours and standard deviation 4 hours.
Alice's calculator requires 4 batteries and will stop working when any one battery reaches the end of its lifetime.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected battery will last for longer than 16 hours.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: for evaluating probability using their calculator (awrt 0.691) Accept 0.6915
$\mathrm{P}(L>16)=0.69146\ldots$ awrt $0.691$ (1)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At the start of her exams Alice put 4 new batteries in her calculator.
She has used her calculator for 16 hours, but has another 4 hours of exams to sit.
(b) Find the probability that her calculator will not stop working for Alice's remaining exams.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for a first step of identifying a suitable conditional probability (either form)
A1ft: for a ratio of probabilities with numerator = awrt 0.309 or $1-$(a) and denom = their (a)
A1: for awrt 0.446 (o.e.) Accept 0.4465 (from $\frac{0.3085}{0.691}=0.44645\ldots$)
NB $\frac{\mathrm{P}(16<L<20)}{\mathrm{P}(L>16)}=0.5538\ldots$ scores M1A1A1 when they do $1-0.5538=0.4462\ldots$
dM1: (dep on 1st M1) for 2nd correct step i.e. their $0.446\ldots^4$ or $X \sim \mathrm{B}(4,\text{"}0.446\text{"})$ and $\mathrm{P}(X=4)$
A1: for awrt $0.0396$
$\mathrm{P}(L>20|L>16)=\frac{\mathrm{P}(L>20)}{\mathrm{P}(L>16)}=\frac{0.308537\ldots}{(a)}$ or $1-(a),=0.44621\ldots$
For calc to work require $(0.44621\ldots)^4=0.03964\ldots$ awrt $0.0396$ (5)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Alice only has 2 new batteries so, after the first 16 hours of her exams, although her calculator is still working, she randomly selects 2 of the batteries from her calculator and replaces these with the 2 new batteries.
(c) Show that the probability that her calculator will not stop working for the remainder of her exams is 0.199 to 3 significant figures.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for a correct approach to solving the problem (May be implied by A1ft)
A1ft: for $\mathrm{P}(L>4)=$ awrt 0.9998 used and ft their 0.44621 in correct expression
If use $\mathrm{P}(L>20)=0.3085\ldots$ as $0.446\ldots$ in (b) then M1 for $(0.3085\ldots)^2 \times [\mathrm{P}(L>4)]^2$; A1ft as above
A1cso*: for 0.199 or better with clear evidence of M1 [NB $(0.4662\ldots)^2=0.199\ldots$ is M0A0A0] Must see M1 scored by correct expression in symbols or values (M1A1ft)
Require: $[\mathrm{P}(L>4)]^2 \times [\mathrm{P}(L>20|L>16)]^2 = (0.99976\ldots)^2 \times (\text{"}0.44621\ldots\text{"})^2 = 0.19901\ldots$ awrt $\underline{0.199}$ $(\ast)$ (3)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
After her exams, Alice believed that the lifetime of the batteries was more than 18 hours. She took a random sample of 20 of these batteries and found that their mean lifetime was 19.2 hours.
(d) Stating your hypotheses clearly and using a 5% level of significance, test Alice's belief.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) B1: for both hypotheses in terms of $\mu$: $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu=18$   $\mathrm{H_1}: \mu>18$
M1: for selecting a suitable model. Sight of normal, mean 18, sd $\frac{4}{\sqrt{20}}$ (o.e.) or variance $=0.8$
1st A1: for using the model correctly. Allow awrt 0.0899 or 0.09 from correct prob statement
2nd A1: for correct non-contextual conclusion. Wrong comparison or contradictions A0
Error giving 2nd A0 implies 3rd A0 but just a correct contextual conclusion can score A1A1
3rd A1: dep on M1 and 1st A1 for a correct contextual conclusion mentioning Alice's claim/belief or that there is insufficient evidence that the mean lifetime is more than 18 hours
ALT: Using CR $(\bar{L})>19.471\ldots$ (accept awrt 19.5) or CV of 1.6449 (or better: calc 1.6448536\ldots)
$\bar{L} \sim \mathrm{N}\left(18,\left(\frac{4}{\sqrt{20}}\right)^2\right)$

At time $t$ seconds, where $t \geqslant 0$, a particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane in such a way that its velocity $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is given by
$\mathbf{v} = t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i} - 4t\mathbf{j}$
When $t=1$, $P$ is at the point $A$ and when $t=4$, $P$ is at the point $B$.
Find the exact distance $AB$.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Integrate $\mathbf{v}$ w.r.t. time. At least one power increasing by 1.
A1: $\mathbf{r}=2t^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{i}-2t^2\mathbf{j}\ (+\mathbf{C})$. Any correct (unsimplified) expression
M1: Substitute $t=4$ and $t=1$ into their $\mathbf{r}$. Must have attempted to integrate $\mathbf{v}$. Substitute $t=4$ and $t=1$ into their $\mathbf{r}$ to produce 2 vectors (or 2 points if just working with coordinates).
A1: $t=4,\mathbf{r}=4\mathbf{i}-32\mathbf{j}\ (+\mathbf{C})$; $t=1,\mathbf{r}=2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}\ (+\mathbf{C})$ or $(4,-32);(2,-2)$. These can be seen or implied.
M1: $\sqrt{2^2+(-30)^2}$. Attempt at distance of form $\sqrt{(x_1-x_2)^2+(y_1-y_2)^2}$ for their points. Must have 2 non-zero terms.
A1: $\sqrt{904}=2\sqrt{226}$ or any equivalent surd (exact answer needed)
Notes: Allow column vectors throughout. (6)

(6)

questions.stem:
[In this question $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively and position vectors are given relative to the fixed point $O$.]

A particle $P$ moves with constant acceleration.
At time $t=0$, the particle is at $O$ and is moving with velocity $(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
At time $t=2$ seconds, $P$ is at the point $A$ with position vector $(7\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ is $2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Use of $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{u}t+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$: $(7\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})=2(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}\cdot 2^2$. Using a complete method to obtain the acceleration. N.B. Equation, in $\mathbf{a}$ only, could be obtained by two integrations
A1: $\mathbf{a}=(1.5\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})$
M1: $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{1.5^2+(-2)^2}$. Attempt to find magnitude of their $\mathbf{a}$ using form $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$
A1*: $=2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ GIVEN ANSWER. Correct GIVEN ANSWER obtained correctly
No credit for individual component calculations
ALTERNATIVE: M1: Use velocity at half-time ($t=1$) = Average velocity over time period. So at $t=1$, $\mathbf{v}=\frac{1}{2}(7\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})$ so $\mathbf{a}=\frac{1}{2}(7\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})-(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})$. N.B. could see $(7\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})=(4\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j})+2\mathbf{a}$ as first line of working
A1: Correct $\mathbf{a}$ vector (4)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At the instant when $P$ leaves the point $A$, the acceleration of $P$ changes so that $P$ now moves with constant acceleration $(4\mathbf{i}+8.8\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
At the instant when $P$ reaches the point $B$, the direction of motion of $P$ is north east.
(b) Find the time it takes for $P$ to travel from $A$ to $B$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Use of $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t=(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})+2(1.5\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})$. Using a complete method to obtain the velocity at $A$, e.g. by use of $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$ with $t=2$ and $\mathbf{u}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ and their $\mathbf{a}$. OR: by use of $\mathbf{s}=\mathbf{v}t-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$. OR: by integrating their $\mathbf{a}$, with addition of $\mathbf{C}=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$, and putting $t=2$
A1: $=(5\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j})$. Correct vector
M1: $\mathbf{v}=(5\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j})+t(4\mathbf{i}+8.8\mathbf{j})=(5+4t)\mathbf{i}+(8.8t-7)\mathbf{j}$ and $(5+4t)=(8.8t-7)$. Complete method to find equation in $t$ only, e.g. by using $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{a}t$, with their $\mathbf{u}$ and equating $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components OR: by integrating $(4\mathbf{i}+8.8\mathbf{j})$, with addition of a constant, and equating $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components. N.B. Must be equating $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components of a velocity vector and must be their velocity at $A$, to give an equation in $t$ only for this M mark
A1: $t=2.5$ (s) (4)

A small block of mass $3M$ is placed on the plank at the point $P$, where $AP=x$.
The plank is in equilibrium in a vertical plane which is perpendicular to the wall.
The angle between the rope and the plank is $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha=\frac{3}{4}$, as shown in Figure 3.
The plank is modelled as a uniform rod, the block is modelled as a particle and the rope is modelled as a light inextensible string.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Using the model, show that the tension in the rope is $\dfrac{5Mg(3x+a)}{6a}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Moments about $A$ (or any other complete method), with usual rules, or any other complete method to obtain an equation in $a,M,x$ and $T$ only.
A1: $T\cdot 2a\sin\alpha=Mga+3Mgx$. Correct equation
A1*: $T=\frac{Mg(a+3x)}{2a\cdot\frac{3}{5}}=\frac{5Mg(3x+a)}{6a}$ GIVEN ANSWER. Correct PRINTED ANSWER, correctly obtained, need to see $\sin\alpha=\frac{3}{5}$ used. (3)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The magnitude of the horizontal component of the force exerted on the plank at $A$ by the wall is $2Mg$.
(b) Find $x$ in terms of $a$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $\frac{5Mg(3x+a)}{6a}\cos\alpha=2Mg$ OR $2Mg\cdot 2a\tan\alpha=Mga+3Mgx$. Using an appropriate strategy to find $x$, e.g. resolve horizontally with usual rules applying OR moments about $C$. Must use the given expression for $T$.
A1: $x=\frac{2a}{3}$. Accept $0.67a$ or better (2)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The force exerted on the plank at $A$ by the wall acts in a direction which makes an angle $\beta$ with the horizontal.
(c) Find the value of $\tan\beta$
(5)
